newsitem.title: ITALY: CRICKET-AND YOU THOUGHT SERIE A WAS ITALIAN SOCCER....
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-AND YOU THOUGHT SERIE A WAS ITALIAN SOCCER....

text.p: Italy's serie A season starts this month.
That may surprise soccer fans who thought it was about to end. They may be even more startled to hear that serie A is all about bowling and batting averages.
Not to mention the occasional googly.

Yes, the start of the Italian cricket season will go unnoticed by the majority of the country, baffled by the rules of the quintessentially English sport -- assuming they have ever heard of it at all.
With the battle for the serie A soccer title an infinitely greater pull on the nation's imagination, Italian cricketers are feeling a bit left out.

"Interest for cricket here is small. With all the players in the same colour and all in the middle of the pitch, Italians don't understand it," Andrea Amati, one of the country's 'star' players, told Reuters.
"They confuse it with croquet or polo."

Whereas the idyllic English summer wouldn't be complete without the sound of leather on willow coming from the village green, most Italians are unwilling to give up a whole Sunday to play a strange game on a sun-burnt, artificial wicket.
"What we're struggling on is the culture of cricket," said Simone Gambino, chairman of the Italian Cricket Federation.
The federation's official report for the 1996 season shows five men in white flannels celebrating an impressive Italian victory over Argentina.
But the names of the five who helped overpower the South American team give the game away a bit: Akhlaq Quereshi, Kamal Kariyawasan, Razzaq, Sajjad and Javed.
With only a few hundred registered Italian players, the national squad has to look to Pakistan and Sri Lanka for inspiration, finding foreign players part-time jobs as payment.
Como Cricket Club in the north of the country is a case in point. With all of its players from Asia it can hardly claim to represent a growth in Italian cricket.
Another club phoned the Sri Lankan embassy to arrange for two players to be sent over to Italy to bolster its weak side. Not surprisingly, the team is now one of the strongest in Italy.
Even in the past, Italian cricket was never really all that Italian, being introduced onto the peninsula by English expatriates late last century.

Serie A soccer club Juventus was known in a previous incarnation before football arrived as the International Cricket and Football Club of Turin but the cricketing element died out as English influence waned.
So why do the few die-hard Italians involved in cricket on the peninsula continue to strive against all the odds for national recognition?
Gambino gives a clue in the lighthearted way he brushes off questions about the future of the game.
In the end, it's only for fun, he says.

"The majority want to play social cricket as if they were professionals," Gambino said, refering to the fact that most club players do not take the game all that seriously but like the kudos of playing in a national league.
"Italy is a soccer-minded culture where people play cricket because they like to say they play serie A".
The recent routing of the national squad by Bermuda, Hong Kong and Scotland in the 1999 World Cup qualifying tournament in Malaysia would have shattered any delusions of grandeur.
Gambino was realistic in his assessment that most of his players would come back demoralised from Asia and may not even want to play the three-month season.
"Most players will be very demotivated," he said. But it was not all doom and gloom.
He said Italy had to build on local talent such as Amati, who started playing cricket after joining some children for an impromptu game while learning English in Cambridge.
"We have to find those Italians who are playing cricket in England and bring them back here to give the sport time to develop," Gambino said.
Besides scouring England for cricket-playing Italians, the federation is also desperately trying to make the game a truly national sport.
Gambino said efforts have been made to cut dependence on foreign players by allowing only four non-Italians per team and by rules that they not bat together or bowl consecutive overs.
In the case of teams such as Como where all the players are foreign, however, this has proved a bit difficult and exceptions have had to be made to stop clubs dying out.
Amati estimated around 4,000 Italians could be playing cricket soon but others are more pessimistic for the future.
Gambino said it would take years to develop cricket and doubted the game would ever grow deep roots in Italy. "It will be a long, long, long, slow, slow, slow process," he said.
